extracted.intended_audience: National Science Foundation program officers, MER co-directors, AERA/NSF evaluation stakeholders, and researchers evaluating professional networks in mathematics education
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of the Mathematicians and Education Reform (MER) Forum focused on how the network influences participants' involvement in mathematics-education reform (postsecondary and K-12), and the program's effectiveness, reach, communications, workshops, and systemic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which MER reaches its target audience of research mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether MER reaches its target audience of research mathematicians (the academic mathematics community in four-year colleges and universities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic and participation data (e.g., percent tenured faculty, representation of women and minorities, workshop and newsletter reach). Note that MER attracts a relatively narrow slice of mathematicians and misconceptions about exclusivity persist; consider both absolute numbers (mailing list size, workshop attendees) and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of the Forum's communication activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the effectiveness of MER's communication avenues (workshops, word of mouth, newsletters, special mailings, posted announcements, special sessions, listserver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure which channels attract new members vs which keep existing members informed. Example findings: word of mouth was reported as most effective for recruitment (34% mathematicians; 50% math educators/K-12), newsletters informative to those already in the network but rarely a primary recruitment source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and depth of MER's educational initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the topical coverage and depth of MER initiatives across K-12, undergraduate, graduate, and systemic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize workshop/session topics (general issues; direct connections with K-12; university issues; K-12 issues; systemic issues). Track shifts over time (e.g., from K-12 focus toward undergraduate/calculus reform) and frequency of topic coverage; evaluate whether the initiatives are superficial introductions or substantive/deep engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of MER's workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the workshops' effects on participants' knowledge, attitudes, networks, and behavior (including reported changes in their educational efforts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use participant surveys, attendance rates, qualitative reports: reported benefits include validating existing ideas, learning new applicable information, networking/contacts, and classroom changes. Note that many participants find face-to-face exchanges and informal interactions most valuable. Also evaluate whether workshops model reform pedagogy (participants requested more modeling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which MER meets needs of mathematicians and mathematics and K-12 educators
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how well MER addresses the needs of its multiple constituencies (research mathematicians, mathematics educators, K-12 teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey items asking perceived usefulness, whether MER duplicates other organizations, and whether participants feel supported. Consider differential effects across groups (e.g., mathematicians vs math-educators vs K-12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic effects of MER's activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess MER's influence beyond individuals—on departments, institutional policies, and larger systemic reform efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for indicators of departmental and institutional change (curricular changes, pedagogy adoption, institutional support/rewards), and document degree of systemic versus individual-level impact. Recognize that systemic change is more difficult and slower; MER's primary impact may be at individual and departmental leadership levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: MER's functional role: facilitator/supporter versus initiator
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether MER primarily facilitates and supports mathematicians already involved in reform, or whether it initiates new reform activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors treat MER as a facilitator/supporter—'taking people where they are'—and recommend using that conception of effectiveness; avoid using overly stringent criteria that expect MER to originate broad institutional change alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic composition and inclusiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure participant demographics (rank, tenure status, gender, race/ethnicity) and assess inclusiveness of MER relative to the broader mathematics community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey demographics: e.g., 77% tenured faculty, women 27% (vs 20% in broader community), ~90% white. Evaluate whether MER's membership reflects intended diversity goals and whether perceived exclusivity limits reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of participants' time and role balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how participants allocate time among research, teaching, educational reform, service, and administration, and how these allocations compare to departmental expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-reported hours and percent time data; examine gender differences (e.g., women reported more time on teaching and reform than men) and tensions between research expectations and reform activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication channel performance by audience segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate which communication methods work best for each target group (mathematicians, math-educators, K-12 teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the study: word of mouth effective across groups; posted announcements more effective for K-12; special mailings had varying effectiveness. Consider tailoring channels to audience and leveraging effective informal networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of the MER newsletter and publication outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the newsletter's usefulness for information dissemination, member engagement, and recruitment, and evaluate awareness/usefulness of CBMS Issues volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure readership, perceived helpful sections (feature articles, essays, summaries), and recruitment effect (few learned MER via newsletter). For CBMS volumes, measure awareness and perceived usefulness across constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of special sessions and banquet at Joint Meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the role of special sessions and the banquet in raising visibility of education within professional meetings, providing information, networking, and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure attendance rates and perceived benefits: learning new information, making contacts, finding support. Note that special sessions did not often influence decision to attend the Joint Meeting or MER workshop; banquet widely recommended by attendees as networking venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop design quality (pedagogical modeling and interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate workshop structure and pedagogy—extent to which workshops model reform-oriented pedagogy and provide interactive, informal exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants valued face-to-face exchanges and informal interactions; many requested more modeling of reform pedagogy in breakout sessions. Consider including demonstrations of non-traditional pedagogy during sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus alignment and topical emphasis (K-12 vs undergraduate vs graduate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether MER's topical focus aligns with program goals and participant needs, noting any shifts in emphasis over time (e.g., toward undergraduate/calculus reform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track frequency of workshop topics, changes in newsletter focus, and participant involvement levels across areas. Evaluate whether broadening focus promotes cross-level collaboration (e.g., teacher preparation bridging K-12 and undergraduate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Building bridges with mathematics education community
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate MER's success at forging connections between research mathematicians and mathematics educators/K-12 teachers to maximize impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for participation of math-educators and teachers at workshops, advisory board representation (e.g., NCTM figures), interdisciplinary team applications, and whether MER facilitates communication across communities via workshops and networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-reported benefits: awareness and legitimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure participant perceptions of benefits such as increased awareness of educational issues and legitimization of education work within the mathematics research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey items asking if MER made respondents more aware of issues (examples: calculus reform, technology use, teacher preparation) and whether MER provided legitimization/support for educational interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-reported benefits: supportive atmosphere and networking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether MER creates a supportive network where participants feel comfortable contacting colleagues about professional matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure proportions reporting comfort contacting MER colleagues (survey showed >70% agreement) and frequency of post-workshop contacts on teaching, reform, and research topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-reported benefits: changes to classroom pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess self-reported changes in teaching practices attributable (directly or indirectly) to MER participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey questions ask whether participants changed their teaching and whether they attribute changes to MER newsletters/workshops/networking. Common changes include cooperative learning, increased technology use (graphing calculators, Mathematica, MAPLE), hands-on activities, participatory classes, and adoption of reformed curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental indicators of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure departmental-level changes indicating increased valuation of education reform: curricular changes, attention to pedagogy, institutional support, and rewards for educational work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document examples (adoption of reform calculus, new entry-level or graduate pedagogy courses, remedial education reform, support for emerging scholars). Assess proportion of faculty involved in reform and whether departments provide institutional rewards/recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to systemic change and institutional culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify structural and cultural barriers within academia that limit systemic reform (e.g., emphasis on individual research over collaborative curricular work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative data to document cultural resistance, tenure/promotion expectations, and the need for department-level incentives. Recognize that supporting individuals is necessary but insufficient for cultural change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of the Departmental Network
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the newer departmental component of MER in fostering departmental-level education reform at research universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect site-visit data, examine departmental initiatives, compare departmental network activities to individual network impacts, and note that the departmental network was newer and findings shorter/smaller-scale in this evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology and triangulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple methods and data sources to triangulate findings (surveys of all participants, site visits, participant observation, interviews, document review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ both qualitative (coding, domain analysis) and quantitative (descriptive/inferential statistics) methods. Note response rates (e.g., 230/730 = ~32%) and limitations of self-report data; combine data sources to strengthen claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant involvement metrics across reform activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure self-reported level of involvement in a list of reform activities (e.g., K-12 curriculum reform, undergraduate curriculum reform, calculus reform, pre-service/in-service programs, recruitment of underrepresented groups, graduate education reform, district/state initiatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a four-point involvement scale (not at all, a little, considerably, very) as in the MER questionnaire; analyze differences by gender and other demographics (examples: females more involved in K-12-related activities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and attendance motivation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess why participants attend MER workshops (colleague recommendation, department chair, invited speaker, desire to meet peers, interest in theme, cost/expense incentives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use checklist items from workshop questionnaires to identify primary recruitment channels and incentives; use willingness-to-attend questions under different expense scenarios to estimate future participation probabilities.
